## Setting Up the Problem (Bayes' Theorem)

**Given information:**
- Prevalence: P(Disease) = 1/500 = 0.002, so P(No Disease) = 0.998
- Sensitivity: P(Test+ | Disease) = 0.98
- Specificity: P(Test− | No Disease) = 0.95, so P(Test+ | No Disease) = 0.05 (false positive rate)

**Step 1: Compute P(Test+), the total probability of a positive test**

P(Test+) = P(Test+|Disease)·P(Disease) + P(Test+|No Disease)·P(No Disease)

P(Test+) = (0.98 × 0.002) + (0.05 × 0.998)
P(Test+) = 0.00196 + 0.0499
P(Test+) = 0.05186

**Step 2: Apply Bayes' Theorem**

P(Disease | Test+) = [P(Test+|Disease) · P(Disease)] / P(Test+)

P(Disease | Test+) = 0.00196 / 0.05186

P(Disease | Test+) = 0.0377941...

**Step 3: Convert to percentage**

0.0377941 × 100 = 3.77941...%

Rounded to two decimal places: **3.78%**

**Sanity check:** Out of 500,000 people (a convenient large multiple), we'd expect 1,000 true cases. True positives = 1,000 × 0.98 = 980. Among the 499,000 healthy people, false positives = 499,000 × 0.05 = 24,950. Total positives = 980 + 24,950 = 25,930. PPV = 980 / 25,930 = 0.037794... = 3.78%. ✓ Matches.

This illustrates the classic base-rate effect: even with a good test (98% sensitivity, 95% specificity), because the condition is rare, most positive results are still false positives.

FINAL ANSWER: 3.78
